Coefficient Omega (McDonald) With a Confidence Interval

Source: R/reliability_omega.R
reliability_omega.Rd

Estimates McDonald's (1999) coefficient \(\omega\) for a homogeneous composite score from a single-factor confirmatory factor analysis model and returns a confidence interval for the population coefficient. The denominator argument selects whether the total variance in the denominator of \(\omega\) is estimated directly from the data ("observed", the default: robust omega) or taken from the fitted model ("model_implied"); see Details for the properties of each choice. A bootstrap confidence interval is never run unless requested; see ci_method.

Usage

reliability_omega(
  data = NULL,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  ci_method = c("mlr_logistic", "ml_logistic", "mlr", "ml", "likelihood", "adf",
    "adf_logistic", "feldt", "fisher", "bonett", "hakstian_whalen", "bootstrap_se",
    "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", "bca", "none"),
  denominator = c("observed", "model_implied"),
  missing = c("fiml", "listwise", "two_stage"),
  aux = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  B = 10000,
  seed = NULL,
  ncpus = 1L,
  improper = c("keep", "drop"),
  wald_df = Inf,
  progress = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A numeric matrix or data frame of item scores (rows are respondents, columns are items). Either data or S must be supplied. How incomplete rows are handled is governed by missing: full information maximum likelihood by default, listwise deletion with missing = "listwise", or two-stage maximum likelihood with missing = "two_stage". When aux is supplied, data contains both the item columns and the auxiliary columns, and the columns not named in aux are the items. An item column that is not numeric (or logical), and an item that takes a single value in the rows analyzed (the complete rows under listwise deletion, the rows that observe it otherwise), are refused by name before anything is computed, as is a zero variance on the diagonal of S: such an item adds a constant to the composite, whose reliability it leaves as it is, while the coefficient would count it among the \(J\) items (alpha with it is \(J(J-2)/(J-1)^2\) times alpha without it). A composite that does not vary is refused too, as when the items are ipsative (their scores sum to the same total in every row): its reliability is not defined. Under missing = "fiml" and "two_stage" it is checked in the rows that observe every item when they outnumber the items, where a composite that does not vary leaves the likelihood of the saturated model without a maximum, and otherwise on the EM estimate of the covariance matrix. In holzinger_swineford, t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, and t4_lozenges, each centered on the pupil's mean of the three, are ipsative items of this kind. SPSS user-defined missing values, which haven::read_sav(user_na = TRUE) keeps as values of a haven_labelled_spss column, are missing, as SPSS treats them.

S

A symmetric covariance matrix among the items. If supplied, N must also be supplied; methods that require raw data ("mlr*", "adf*", "bootstrap_*", "percentile", "bca") are then unavailable, as are missing = "fiml" and missing = "two_stage" named explicitly, and aux, since a covariance matrix has no incomplete cases (the default of missing analyzes it as it stands).

N

Total sample size; required when S is supplied.

ci_method

Method for constructing the confidence interval. See Details. When not supplied (or passed as NULL): for denominator = "model_implied" the default is "mlr_logistic" with raw data, the robust maximum likelihood standard error with the limits formed on the logit scale and transformed back (Browne, 1982; Kelley, 2007a), whatever the treatment of missing values, except under wald_df = "missing_information", where it is "mlr", the same standard error with the limits formed on the scale of omega, the interval that rule is calibrated for; with covariance input, which the robust standard error cannot use, it is "ml_logistic", the maximum likelihood standard error with the limits formed the same way ("ml" under wald_df = "missing_information"); for denominator = "observed" (robust omega) no interval is computed by default, because its interval is bootstrap based and a bootstrap is never run unless requested. Ask for "percentile" or "bca" to obtain the recommended interval. The closed forms, the Wald intervals, and the profile likelihood apply to denominator = "model_implied" only; a combination that does not apply stops with a message naming the denominator that does (see Details).

denominator

How the total variance in the denominator of \(\omega\) is estimated: "observed" (default; robust omega) uses the variance of the composite estimated directly from the data; "model_implied" uses the total variance reproduced by the fitted single-factor model. See Details. With "observed", ci_method must be a bootstrap method or "none".

missing

How incomplete rows of data are handled: "fiml" (the default; full information maximum likelihood, using every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable), "listwise" (complete-case analysis), or "two_stage" (two-stage maximum likelihood, using the same cases as FIML). The default analysis is FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise, unlike fa_confirmatory, which fits complete data by FIML too: data in which no value is missing, data complete but for rows with every item missing (which both treatments drop), and S are analyzed as they stand, since the complete-data intervals need that analysis; incomplete items are analyzed by FIML, or, when ci_method names an interval FIML cannot give, the call stops and names the choices. See Details. With missing = "listwise", when fewer than two rows are complete, listwise deletion leaves nothing to analyze, and the function stops before any fit, says so, and names the treatment that uses the incomplete rows. The single-factor model is fit by maximum likelihood, which needs the covariance matrix positive definite, and \(N\) complete rows give a matrix of rank at most \(N - 1\), so with no more complete rows than items the function stops the same way; reliability_alpha, which needs only the sums of the matrix, is computed from two or more complete rows. Full information maximum likelihood does not impose an ordinary complete-case count rule. Observed-denominator omega and two-stage estimation require unrestricted moments, checked for affine collapse or numerical instability as described in cov_fiml. EM convergence alone does not establish existence or uniqueness. Model-implied omega can retain a proper identified constrained FIML fit and H0-based uncertainty while withholding unavailable H1 diagnostics and residual correlations. The result states this qualification. Bootstrap resamples retain a distinct-case estimability screen as a separate policy, not a universal likelihood-existence theorem. Listwise complete rows are counted as distinct rows. Two columns of one name are refused before any of this, under every treatment, since the items are read by name.

aux

Optional character vector naming auxiliary variable columns of data: entered as saturated correlates under full information maximum likelihood, and into the first stage under missing = "two_stage". Supplying aux without missing implies missing = "fiml". See Details.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval. Defaults to 0.95.

B

Number of bootstrap replications when a bootstrap method is selected, a single whole number. Defaults to 10000. The fewest accepted depends on the interval method and the level: at the default conf_level, 400 for "percentile" (10 replications beyond each limit), 2000 for "bca" (50 beyond each nominal limit, because the adjusted limits sit farther into the tails), and 100 for "bootstrap_se" and "bootstrap_se_logistic" (a standard deviation of the replications); at 0.99 the first two are 2000 and 10000. A smaller B is refused before anything is computed (class dmar_count_invalid). The count is held to the number requested. Replications set aside afterward are counted and reported in a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped, which names the function and says to request more when those that return a value are fewer than the number required; when fewer than half of the B replications return a value, the interval is withheld (limits and bootstrap standard error NA) under a warning of class dmar_bootstrap_insufficient. See dmar_bootstrap, which also describes options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) for a first look with a smaller B.

seed

Random number seed used for bootstrap reproducibility. Defaults to NULL, under which the resamples are drawn from, and advance, the current random number stream; supply an integer for a reproducible interval, which is set for the call only, the caller's random number state being restored when it returns.

ncpus

The number of processes over which the bootstrap replications are spread. The default 1 runs them in this R session; a larger number uses forked workers (boot's parallel = "multicore") or, on Windows, which cannot fork, a socket cluster ("snow"), whose workers load the installed DMAR. boot draws every resample before any replication runs, so a given seed returns the same interval, counts, and replicates whatever ncpus is. A session that forks workers and also starts background processes through callr or processx needs the environment variable PROCESSX_NOTIFY_OLD_SIGCHLD set before processx is loaded (see sem_exact_fit_bootstrap). Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

improper

How a bootstrap replication whose single-factor solution is improper (a negative error variance, a Heywood case) is treated when the solution still yields a coefficient: "keep" (the default) uses its estimate like any other, and "drop" sets it aside. Either way such replications are counted in the bootstrap attribute and the printed line, and a replication whose solution yields no coefficient is set aside under both (see Details). With "drop" an improper point estimate stops the call, since an interval built from proper replications only would not describe it. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

wald_df

The reference distribution of a Wald interval: Inf (the default), the normal distribution; a single positive number, the degrees of freedom of a t distribution; or "missing_information", von Hippel's (2016) degrees of freedom \(\max\{3, N(1 - \gamma) - 1\}\) from omega's fraction of missing information \(\gamma\) (\(N - 1\) with complete data). A number applies to the Wald intervals of the model implied coefficient ("ml", "mlr", "adf", and their _logistic variants), the keyword to "ml" and "mlr" only, without two-stage estimation, the intervals its calibration covers; anything else is an error that says why. See Details.

progress

NULL (the default), or a function of two arguments that the bootstrap calls as it runs, so that an application can show how far a long bootstrap has gone and let its user stop it (a Shiny app, for example). It is called as progress(done, total), with the number of replications attempted so far and B: after each replication when ncpus = 1, and with more processes after each block of replications they complete together, about a fiftieth of B (ncpus * ceiling(B / (50 * ncpus)) replications, the last block possibly fewer), so that done advances by the block. A BCa interval takes its acceleration from a regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications return a value as there are cases, and from the jackknife, one leave-one-out refit per case, when fewer do or when that regression fails or gives influence values that are not all finite; the jackknife runs at most once in a call, and not at all when no interval is formed or every returned replicate has the same value. While it runs, the callback is called again after each refit (with more processes, after each block of ncpus * ceiling(n / (50 * ncpus)) refits, n the number of cases resampled), with done and total both B, so it can be called more than B times, and done equal to total does not mean that the bootstrap has finished. If the callback returns FALSE, the bootstrap stops before the next replication or block with an error of class dmar_bootstrap_cancelled, whose elements done and total say how far it got (see dmar_metadata); any other value is ignored. An error inside the callback stops the call with an error of class dmar_progress_error, whose message names the callback and which carries done, total, and, as parent, the callback's own condition with its class intact, so that an application can tell a failing callback from a failing analysis. The callback runs outside the random number stream, so a given seed returns the same result with or without it, and a callback that draws random numbers leaves the caller's stream as it found it. With NULL nothing is called. Ignored unless a bootstrap method is selected.

Value

A data.frame with columns term and value and rows "estimate" (sample coefficient \(\omega\)), "se" (standard error on the coefficient scale, NA for methods that do not produce one; for the transformation-based intervals "fisher", "bonett", and "hakstian_whalen" it is the delta method back-transform of the transformation-scale standard error), "se_transformed" (only for those transformation-based intervals: the standard error on the transformation scale, with the scale named in the attribute se_transform_scale: "fisher_z", "log(1-alpha)", or "cube_root"), "ci_lower" and "ci_upper" (each clamped into [0, 1], so the limits stay in order), "conf_level", "N" (the cases the analysis used: the complete cases under listwise deletion, and under "fiml" and "two_stage" every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable), "N_complete" (the complete cases; equal to "N" under listwise deletion and for covariance input), and "n_items" (number of items). Attributes coefficient ("omega"), ci_method, denominator, missing, wald_df (the degrees of freedom of the Wald interval's t reference, Inf for the normal one and for intervals that are not Wald intervals; under wald_df = "missing_information" the attribute wald_df_table holds the df_missing table they came from), and (when supplied) aux record the computation; bootstrap calls also record B. The attribute residual_cor carries the local dependence summary of a maximum likelihood fit of the single-factor model to the same cases, whatever the ci_method (the weighted least squares fit behind the ADF intervals has residuals of its own, so it is not used for the summary): a list with matrix (the observed minus the model implied item correlations, named by item), largest (the residual correlation largest in absolute value, with its sign), items (the pair it belongs to), and saturated. With three items the single-factor model is saturated (zero degrees of freedom) and a proper solution reproduces every correlation, so its residuals are zero and carry no information about local dependence: saturated is then TRUE, largest is NA, and items is NULL, rather than naming whichever pair carries the largest rounding error. The printed table names the denominator and the largest residual correlation (or says that the model is saturated) in two lines under the table. A bootstrap call also carries the attribute bootstrap, a list recording the replications the interval conditions on: attempted (B), returned (the replications whose value the interval uses; the standard error is their standard deviation and the percentile and BCa limits are their quantiles), failed (the difference), reasons (a named count of why replications were set aside: error when the refit raised an error, non_finite when it was set aside without one, as a fit that did not converge is, and as an improper one is under improper = "drop" even though its estimate is finite), error_messages (the distinct error messages with their counts, empty when none), undetermined (the replications set aside because the resample left a polychoric correlation undetermined, which only reliability_omega_categorical counts; zero here), improper and improper_kept (the replications whose single-factor solution was improper, with a negative error variance, or with three items had no single-factor solution at all: those set aside, which are among the non_finite ones, and those whose estimate the interval uses, which are among the returned ones), no_solution (the replications of three items set aside because their correlations admit no single-factor solution, a subset of improper), improper_rule ("keep" or "drop"; see the argument improper), not_converged (zero here: a fit that did not converge is counted among the non_finite ones), too_few_cases (the replications set aside because the resample held too few distinct cases for the rule on the number of cases, which are among the error ones; when they number more than half of B, no interval is formed), caution (TRUE when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept number at least \((1 - C)/2\) of B, with \(C\) the confidence level, so that how they were treated can decide where a limit falls), require_half (TRUE: an interval requires at least half of all attempted replications to return defined estimates; this is an estimability safeguard, not a coverage guarantee), required (the fewest replications a request for an interval of this method and level may ask for, a count held to B and not to the replications that return a value: 400 for "percentile", 2000 for "bca", 100 for the two bootstrap standard error methods at the 95 percent level; see dmar_bootstrap), bootstrap_status ("complete", "dropped", "exploratory", "insufficient_count", or "insufficient_share"; under the last two the limits are NA), B_used (the smallest count any reported limit rests on), target_returned and target_withheld (counts and withholding flags for each target in a vector bootstrap), acceleration and acceleration_method (the BCa acceleration used and whether it came from the regression or the jackknife; NA unless a BCa interval was formed), jackknife (the same attempted, returned, failed, reasons, error_messages, undetermined, improper, improper_kept, no_solution, not_converged, and too_few_cases for the leave-one-out refits behind the acceleration, all zero when no jackknife ran), ncpus (the number of processes used), t (the estimate of every replication, in order, NA where there is none; an improper estimate set aside under improper = "drop" is kept here, so the interval under the other rule can be formed without refitting), and status (a factor giving the fate of every replication, with levels "proper", "improper", "error", "non_finite", "undetermined", and "not_converged"). The interval uses the replications whose status is "proper" and, under improper = "keep", those whose status is "improper" and whose t is finite. The attribute B_used is the number of replications the interval uses (returned). The attributes n_dropped (B minus B_used), B_required, and bootstrap_status repeat the counts in the names every bootstrap result of the package carries. The warning has class dmar_bootstrap_replications_dropped when replications were set aside and the interval was formed, and dmar_bootstrap_insufficient when the interval was withheld. A BCa interval is also withheld, with the second class, when fewer than 10 replications lie beyond a limit where the bias correction and the acceleration place it (see dmar_bootstrap). The printed table shows these counts in one line, and a warning states them whenever a replication was set aside or the caution applies.

Details

Coefficient \(\omega\) is a population coefficient of determination. Write the composite \(Y = \sum_j X_j\) through its measurement decomposition, \(Y = E[Y \mid \eta] + e\), the regression of the observed composite on the latent variable \(\eta\) it is intended to measure. By the law of total variance, the proportion of composite variance attributable to \(\eta\) is \(\mathrm{Var}(E[Y \mid \eta]) / \mathrm{Var}(Y)\) (McDonald, 1999, 2011). Under the congeneric single-factor model, in which item \(j\) has factor loading \(\lambda_j\) and error variance \(\psi_j^{2}\), the numerator equals \(\left(\sum_j \lambda_j\right)^2\) and the population coefficient is $$\omega = \frac{\left(\sum_{j} \lambda_{j}\right)^{2}}{\sigma_{Y}^{2}},$$ with \(\sigma_{Y}^{2}\) the variance of the composite. Coefficient \(\omega\) relaxes the equal-loadings assumption underlying coefficient \(\alpha\) (Guttman, 1945; Cronbach, 1951), so on congeneric scales \(\omega\) estimates population reliability whereas \(\alpha\) underestimates it.

The denominator argument. The sample estimate substitutes lavaan estimates of the loadings into the numerator; the two denominator settings differ in how \(\sigma_{Y}^{2}\) is estimated.

"observed" (default)

The variance of the composite estimated directly from the data (the sum of all elements of the unrestricted covariance matrix, on the same maximum likelihood divisor as the fitted loadings). This is the coefficient that Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) call hierarchical omega (MBESS::ci.reliability(type = "hierarchical")); the DMAR documentation refers to it as robust omega, and it is the default because its denominator estimates the variance of the composite consistently whether or not the single-factor model is correctly specified.

"model_implied"

The total variance reproduced by the fitted single-factor model, \(\left(\sum_j \hat\lambda_j\right)^2 + \sum_j \hat\psi_j^{2}\). This is the textbook form of \(\hat\omega\), correct exactly when the one-factor model reproduces the composite variance.

The choice matters only insofar as the single-factor model is misspecified, and the properties of each setting can be stated exactly.

  • If the single-factor model is correctly specified, the two definitions coincide in the population, and both estimators converge to the same value. Nothing is given up, in that sense, by either choice.

  • The observed total variance is a consistent estimator of \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)\) whether or not the single-factor model is correctly specified; the model implied total variance is consistent for \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)\) only when the model is correct.

  • Under misspecification (for example, a minor unmodeled factor or correlated errors), only "observed" retains the coefficient of determination interpretation: the proportion of the variance of the composite users actually compute that is attributable to the fitted common factor. With "model_implied" the estimate becomes a ratio of two model derived quantities whose denominator is no longer the variance of any composite a user scores.

  • Under a correctly specified model with normal items, the model implied denominator uses the model structure and can be a slightly more efficient estimator of \(\sigma_{Y}^{2}\) in finite samples. In the simulations of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) the practical differences between the two coefficients were negligible when the model held, while interval coverage under modest model error favored the observed denominator paired with a bootstrap interval.

Those simulation results are why Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) recommend the observed denominator with a bootstrap confidence interval when unidimensionality is only approximate, which is common with real items.

Stated as one identity, the two denominators differ by \(\mathbf{1}'(\mathbf{S} - \hat{\Sigma})\mathbf{1}\), the sum of every residual covariance of the single-factor fit. The model implied setting treats covariance the model omits as absent from the composite; the observed setting counts it as variance of the composite that the factor does not explain. The first describes the composite as the fitted model describes it, the second the composite users compute. Estimating the factor model from its own implied moments and reporting the reliability of a scored composite with the observed variance are therefore not in tension: the model is needed for the numerator, which partitions the variance of the composite into the part due to the factor and the rest, and is not needed for the denominator, which is the variance of the composite itself. The omega that cfa_1 reports beside the loadings, and that fa_confirmatory reports for continuous items, is the model implied coefficient, a property of the fitted model.

Two cautions frame the choice. First, no denominator repairs a misspecified measurement model: the fitted loadings absorb part of whatever structure the single-factor model omits, so the numerator is affected under either setting. Assess the single-factor model (for example with cfa_1) before interpreting any \(\omega\) variant, and model real multidimensionality directly rather than patching over it. A gap between the two denominators shows that the model does not reproduce the composite variance, but a small gap does not show that the loadings are free of such structure: a doublet or a method factor shared by a few same-signed items inflates their loadings while leaving the two denominators close. The residual correlations of the single-factor fit are where that structure usually shows, so the result carries them (attribute residual_cor; see Value) and the printed table names the largest. One limit applies: when the shared structure sits on the items that dominate the factor, the single factor absorbs it and the misfit appears as residual correlations among the other items, so the largest residual signals local dependence more reliably than it locates it. Second, the naming history is worth knowing. The observed denominator coefficient was introduced as hierarchical omega (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016; MBESS type "hierarchical"), a name motivated by a hierarchical factor logic: model misfit is viewed as a set of minor common factors (visible as residual correlations), the single factor is retained as an approximation, and the coefficient isolates the variance attributable to the general factor alone, expressed relative to the observed variance of the unweighted composite. It is not the bifactor coefficient \(\omega_H\) of Zinbarg, Revelle, Yovel, and Li (2005), whose numerator comes from the general factor loadings of an explicitly multidimensional model. Upon reflection, the authors would have named the coefficient for its behavior rather than for the hierarchical motivation, as observed omega or robust omega; DMAR uses robust omega, with the qualifications that word requires. The robustness is to misspecification of the total variance only, since the numerator remains model based under either denominator; it is not the outlier robustness of Zhang and Yuan (2016), and it is separate from the robust maximum likelihood standard errors available through ci_method. Robust omega also shares a design principle with categorical omega as Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) computed it: in both, the total variance in the denominator is not taken from the fitted factor model. Green and Yang (2009) built the denominator of their categorical coefficient from the model implied polychoric correlations instead, and reliability_omega_categorical offers both through its own denominator argument. The reliability vignette develops this framing.

Available confidence interval methods (set via ci_method):

"ml", "ml_logistic"

Wald interval using the maximum likelihood standard error from lavaan (Raykov, 2002). The _logistic variant applies Browne's (1982) logit transformation (see below).

"mlr", "mlr_logistic"

Wald interval using the robust (Satorra & Bentler, 1994) standard error, recommended among closed-form methods when item distributions deviate from normality (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016). "mlr_logistic" is the default for denominator = "model_implied".

"likelihood"

Profile likelihood interval: the set of population values not rejected by the likelihood ratio test, located by refitting the model under the nonlinear constraint that the model implied reliability equals each candidate value. It respects the [0, 1] range and is not forced to be symmetric about the estimate. Maximum likelihood; available with raw data or covariance input, for denominator = "model_implied" only.

"adf", "adf_logistic"

Wald interval using weighted least squares (“ADF”) estimation (Browne, 1984). Requires raw data and a relatively large sample size.

"feldt", "fisher", "bonett", "hakstian_whalen"

Closed-form intervals derived for coefficient \(\alpha\). They apply mechanically to \(\omega\) but their coverage performance for \(\omega\) is generally inferior to the maximum likelihood and bootstrap intervals (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016).

"bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic", "percentile", "bca"

Nonparametric bootstrap intervals (Efron & Tibshirani, 1993): the rows of data are resampled with replacement B times and \(\omega\) is recomputed, with the factor model refit, on each replication. "percentile" takes the interval limits from the empirical quantiles of the bootstrap estimates; it respects [0, 1] and is not forced to be symmetric about the estimate. "bca" (bias-corrected and accelerated) adjusts the two quantile positions for median bias, estimated from the bootstrap distribution, and for the rate at which the estimator's variance changes with the parameter, the acceleration, estimated by the jackknife; those two adjustments make it second-order accurate where the percentile interval is first-order accurate (DiCiccio & Efron, 1996). The acceleration is estimated as boot estimates it, by regression on the resampling frequencies when at least as many replications as cases returned a value and by the jackknife otherwise, or when that regression fails; a leave-one-out refit that fails is counted and set aside rather than stopping the call, and when the acceleration or the bias correction cannot be estimated at all the percentile interval is returned in its place, with a warning and the substitution recorded in the ci_method attribute; see reliability_omega_categorical for the full account. "bootstrap_se" uses the standard deviation of the bootstrap estimates as a standard error in a normal-theory interval, built on the logit scale for the _logistic variant so the endpoints respect [0, 1] (the standard deviation is carried to the logit scale by the delta method, divided by \(\hat\omega(1 - \hat\omega)\), as in Equation 32 of Kelley and Pornprasertmanit, 2016, and in MBESS::ci.reliability()). When every replication returns the same value, the bootstrap distribution is a single point and every method returns that point at both limits, with a warning (items that are exact linear functions of one variable, which give alpha such replications, do not reach the bootstrap here: their covariance matrix is singular, and the single-factor fit behind the estimate stops on it). Replications whose model refit does not converge are set aside, and so is a replication in which an item takes a single value (a resample that has left out every case on which a rare item differs from the rest), which is refused before the refit, by name, as the data would be, and so is one with no more distinct cases than the rule on the number of cases for the data asks for (see missing; a resample repeats rows, so near the rule's bound many are, and when more than half are no interval is reported, since those left hold more distinct cases than a resample typically does and their spread understates the sampling variability, and at the bound each holds every distinct case; without repeated rows that happens at fewer cases than about 1.65 times the count the rule compares them with); the interval is computed from the replications that return a value, whose quantiles the percentile and BCa limits are; the counts, and why the rest were set aside, travel in the bootstrap attribute (see Value), print under the table, and are stated in a warning whenever a replication was set aside. The default B = 10000 is an accuracy choice: the BCa adjustment pushes the working quantiles farther into the tails of the bootstrap distribution than the percentile interval uses, and stabilizing them takes more replications than the customary 2000; reduce B for exploration, not for a reported analysis. Recommended when assumptions of parametric methods are questionable. Each replication refits the single-factor model by maximum likelihood: robust maximum likelihood has the same estimates and differs only in the standard errors and the test statistic, which a replication does not use, so the robust fit is not repeated B times. Requires raw data and the boot package; supply seed for run-to-run reproducibility, and ncpus to spread the replications over several processes, which leaves the interval for a given seed unchanged. How replications with an improper solution are treated is described next.

"none"

Return only the point estimate.

Which intervals apply to which denominator.

denominator = "model_implied"

Every method on the menu: the Wald intervals "ml", "mlr", and "adf" with their _logistic variants, the profile "likelihood" interval, the alpha-derived closed forms "feldt", "fisher", "bonett", and "hakstian_whalen", the four bootstrap methods, and "none".

denominator = "observed" (robust omega, the default)

The four bootstrap methods ("percentile", "bca", "bootstrap_se", "bootstrap_se_logistic") and "none" only. The delta method standard errors, the profile likelihood, and the alpha-derived closed forms are derived under the model implied ratio and do not account for sampling of the observed denominator, so "mlr_logistic", the default interval of the model implied coefficient, is not an interval for robust omega.

A request for a combination that does not apply, such as ci_method = "mlr" with the default denominator, stops with a message naming the denominator that does; nothing falls back silently. Covariance input (S) and the incomplete data methods (missing = "fiml" and "two_stage") narrow the menu further, as the S argument and the paragraphs on missing data below describe, and each stops the same way. The pairing of robust omega with the bootstrap is not a limitation in practice, since the bootstrap is the interval Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) recommend for the observed denominator coefficient in any case. Because no analysis in DMAR runs a bootstrap unless the user requests one, the default for robust omega is the point estimate with no interval, accompanied by a message naming the call that produces the recommended interval; request ci_method = "percentile" or "bca" to obtain it.

Limits on the scale of omega or on the logit scale. The Wald intervals come in two forms, both built from the same standard error. "ml", "mlr", and "adf" take the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times the standard error, an interval symmetric about the estimate whose upper limit can pass one (the limits are then clamped into [0, 1]; see Value). Their _logistic variants form the limits on the logit scale, \(\log\{\hat\omega / (1 - \hat\omega)\}\), whose standard error the delta method gives as \(\mathrm{SE} / \{\hat\omega (1 - \hat\omega)\}\), and transform them back (Browne, 1982): the limits of a monotone transformation of a parameter are the transformation of its limits, the confidence interval transformation principle that Kelley (2007a) sets out. The interval then lies within (0, 1) and is asymmetric near one, as the sampling distribution of a high reliability is; the se row is the standard error of \(\hat\omega\) itself under either form. The default is "mlr_logistic" on the evidence of a Monte Carlo study (in the package's source repository, methodology/reliability_limits) of factors of three to six items with N from 50 to 500. The study formed both kinds of limits from the same standard error, the normal theory maximum likelihood one for normal data and the Huber-White one of MLR for nonnormal data, so what it compared is the scale on which the limits are formed. With normal data, under listwise deletion and FIML alike, the logit limits covered from .939 to .956 in every cell (a mean absolute departure from .95 of .003), where the limits on the scale of omega covered from .910 to .952 (.009 to .010), their misses falling mostly on one side, with the population value below the lower limit. With nonnormal data fitted by MLR both forms covered below .95, the logit form by less (a mean absolute departure of .013 against .022). No cell used the robust.sem standard error that "mlr_logistic" takes with complete data; it estimates the same asymptotic variance as the Huber-White one, which the default takes under FIML. fa_confirmatory forms the limits of its omega row the same way, and reliability_H those of H by default, so the three give limits of one form. With a covariance matrix, which the robust standard error cannot use, the default is "ml_logistic", as in reliability_H. Under wald_df = "missing_information" the default is "mlr" ("ml" with a covariance matrix), since that rule is calibrated for the intervals on the scale of omega only (see below).

A t reference distribution for the Wald intervals. The Wald intervals ("ml", "mlr", "adf", and their _logistic variants) are the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times its standard error. The normal quantile treats the standard error as known, which it is only in the limit; in small samples, and more so when values are missing, such intervals are too short. Von Hippel (2016, pp. 431–433) showed this for maximum likelihood estimates from incomplete data and proposed keeping the estimate and its standard error while replacing the normal quantile with a t quantile (his Eq. 29). The argument wald_df does that: the interval becomes \(\hat{\omega} \pm t_{1 - \alpha/2, \nu} \mathrm{SE}\) with \(\nu\) the value of wald_df, and for the _logistic variants the t quantile is applied on the logit scale before the limits are transformed back. The default, Inf, is the normal reference. A number is the analyst's own choice of degrees of freedom, best used to see how much a plausible range of them would lengthen the interval; with a few hundred cases the answer is very little (on 200 degrees of freedom the 95% quantile is 1.972 rather than 1.960).

The calibration study described next selected its simulated data sets by an eligibility rule that keeps some draws the affine-collapse diagnostic sets aside, so its results are conditional on that rule, and coverage under the diagnostic's selection has not been established by that study. A raw-data eligibility replay alone cannot validate the FMI refits and information diagnostics. The keyword is an approximate, opt-in rule, not a coverage guarantee.

The keyword wald_df = "missing_information" takes the degrees of freedom from omega's own fraction of missing information \(\gamma\) by von Hippel's (2016, Eqs. 31 and 34) effective sample size rule with \(k = 1\), $$\nu = \max\{3, N(1 - \gamma) - 1\},$$ where \(N\) is the number of cases the fit used and \(\gamma\) is estimated from the fit as fraction_missing_information estimates it; with complete data (listwise deletion, or a covariance matrix) \(\gamma = 0\) and \(\nu = N - 1\). The rule comes from a calibration study of these intervals under full information maximum likelihood (in the package's source repository, methodology/missing_data; fa_confirmatory describes its design), which simulated the model implied omega of one factor models with six items (N from 30 to 200) or 12 (N = 50 and 100), normal data fit by ML and nonnormal data by MLR. Over the cells with \(N \le 100\) and missing values the coverage of the t interval was .0180 from .95 on average, against .0242 for the normal one, and no higher than .9550 in any cell, with normal theory standard errors ("ml") and Huber-White ones ("mlr") alike; with nonnormal data both intervals still covered below .95, the t one less so. On the logit scale the rule did not pass: with normal data the _logistic interval on the normal reference was already within .0044 of .95 on average, and the t reference raised its coverage as high as .9645, above the .96 the study allowed. The keyword therefore applies to ci_method = "ml" and "mlr" only (with ci_method not supplied, the interval is "mlr", or "ml" with a covariance matrix), under listwise deletion or missing = "fiml", and is an error with the _logistic variants, with "adf" and "adf_logistic" (the study evaluated maximum likelihood standard errors only), with two-stage estimation (for which no fraction of missing information is computed), and with every interval that is not a Wald interval. The study fit no auxiliary variables: with aux the rule takes omega's fraction of missing information from the fit that carries them, which is smaller when they predict the missing values, and the study supports that case by analogy rather than directly. Under listwise deletion the standard errors here come from the expected information ("ml", from a covariance matrix too) and the robust.sem sandwich ("mlr", which needs raw data), where the study's cells without missing values used the observed information and the Huber-White sandwich; for omega at N = 30 and 50 they are shorter by less than 1 and by 1 to 2 percent, so the complete data intervals are, if anything, slightly shorter than those the study evaluated. The printed table names the reference distribution in a line under it, under the keyword with N and the FMI; the wald_df attribute records the degrees of freedom, and under the keyword the wald_df_table attribute holds the df_missing table they came from.

Missing data and auxiliary variables. By default (missing = "fiml") incomplete data are analyzed by full information maximum likelihood (FIML), which keeps every case with at least one observed item or observed auxiliary variable and fits the single-factor model to all of them, consistent and efficient under the missing at random (MAR) assumption; missing = "listwise" fits the complete rows alone. Under the default, the model implied omega here and the omega fa_confirmatory reports for the same items agree on incomplete data, the estimate and, with ci_method = "ml_logistic", the interval; the default interval, "mlr_logistic", forms its limits the same way from the robust standard error. Data in which no value is missing, and a covariance matrix, are analyzed as they stand: FIML would give the same estimate, and the standard errors and intervals come from the expected information (and for "mlr" the robust.sem sandwich) where FIML takes the observed information (and the Huber-White sandwich). A row with every item missing does not count as incomplete data: without auxiliary variables, listwise deletion and FIML both drop it, so data that are complete but for such rows (a blank line at the end of a spreadsheet, say) are analyzed as they stand too. The default analysis is therefore FIML whenever an item value is missing and the complete data analysis otherwise. fa_confirmatory differs: it fits complete data by FIML as well. The complete data analysis is used here because the closed-form intervals ("feldt", "fisher", "bonett", "hakstian_whalen"), "adf", "adf_logistic", and "likelihood" need it, FIML giving none of them. On complete data the standard error of omega from fa_confirmatory therefore differs slightly from the one here: by 0.4 percent for t1_visual_perception, t2_cubes, t3_paper_form_board, and t4_lozenges in holzinger_swineford. When the default meets incomplete items and one of those intervals, the call stops rather than deleting cases unasked, and names the two choices: missing = "listwise", which computes the interval from the complete rows alone, or an interval FIML gives ("ml", "mlr", their _logistic variants, or a bootstrap method). The aux argument names auxiliary variables: columns of data that are not part of the composite but are correlated with the items or with the reasons values are missing. They enter as saturated correlates (Graham, 2003): correlated freely with each other and with every item's residual, never loading on the factor, so the measurement model is undisturbed while FIML uses their information; a good auxiliary also makes MAR itself more plausible (Collins, Schafer, & Kam, 2001). A case whose items are all missing is kept when an auxiliary variable is observed on it: the model estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly, so such a case informs the item moments through its auxiliaries, and setting it aside would make the analysis conditional on having an observed item, which biases the estimates when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliaries. Supplying aux without missing implies missing = "fiml", whether or not a value is missing; combining it with an explicit missing = "listwise" is an error. Under missing = "fiml" the denominators are estimated as follows: with "model_implied" the fitted FIML model supplies the total variance directly, and with "observed" the total variance is the sum of the FIML estimate of the item covariance matrix (the EM estimate under a saturated model over the items and any auxiliaries, the matrix cov_fiml returns), which is the estimate of \(\mathrm{Var}(Y)\) that uses the partially observed rows; it is already on the maximum likelihood divisor, matching the fitted loadings. The available intervals under "fiml" are "ml", "mlr" (Yuan & Bentler, 2000, robust), their _logistic variants, and the bootstrap methods, which resample rows including the partially observed ones and refit by FIML; the complete-data closed forms, "adf", and "likelihood" are errors rather than silent fallbacks to listwise deletion.

missing = "two_stage" estimates in two stages instead (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009): the means and covariances of the items are first estimated by maximum likelihood under the saturated normal model (the EM estimates, the same saturated estimate FIML's observed denominator uses), and the single-factor model is then fit to them by the complete data maximum likelihood discrepancy function. The auxiliary variables named in aux enter the first stage only, where they inform the estimated moments, and the measurement model is fit as if they were absent, which is simpler than the saturated correlates FIML needs. Two-stage estimation uses the cases FIML uses, every case with an observed item or an observed auxiliary variable: the first stage estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly, so a case observed on an auxiliary alone informs the item moments through it, and setting such a case aside would condition the analysis on an observed item and bias the estimates when the items went missing together at random given the auxiliaries. lavaan's two-stage estimator reads such a case in its first stage but leaves it out of its sample size, which would make its standard errors too large; the fits go through fa_confirmatory, which computes them again with every case the first stage read, and a message counts such cases (when a fit cannot be computed again, a warning says that the standard error is too large and that a bootstrap interval counts every case). The estimates are consistent under MAR and only marginally less efficient than FIML's (Savalei & Bentler, 2009), and with incomplete nonnormal data Savalei and Falk (2014) found the coverage of robust two-stage intervals better than that of robust FIML intervals. With "model_implied" the "ml" interval uses the normal theory two-stage standard error (Savalei & Bentler, 2009, Eq. 6) and "mlr" the standard error robust to nonnormality (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; lavaan's missing = "robust.two.stage"); with "observed" the numerator comes from the two-stage loadings and the denominator from the EM covariance matrix, so the coefficient differs from its FIML counterpart only through the loadings, and its interval is a bootstrap that refits both stages on every replication. A delta method interval for that coefficient can be derived under two-stage estimation, but its behavior has not been studied, so it is not offered. With three items the single-factor model is saturated and two-stage estimation gives the FIML estimate and standard error. The intervals that FIML refuses are refused here too, and "likelihood" for a further reason: no likelihood of the observed data is maximized. Multiple imputation is a different feature with a different interface and is out of scope here.

Both methods need the covariance of every pair of items and auxiliary variables, and the data carry no information about the covariance of a pair that no case observes together: lavaan only warns, and its EM returns an arbitrary value for it. Nor do they carry any about how two variables vary together when the cases that observe both hold a single value of one of them (or are one case): the estimate of their covariance then rests on the form of the normal model rather than on the data, or is not determined at all. Either pair is refused by name before any fit, with a pointer to missing_coverage, and a refusal of listwise deletion offers missing = "fiml" only when the data hold no such pair. In a bootstrap, a resample that leaves such a pair (or, for the BCa acceleration, a jackknife deletion that does) is set aside with the same message and counted, under either method.

Improper solutions. A single-factor fit can converge to an improper solution, one with a negative error variance (a Heywood case). McDonald (2004), following van Driel (1978), separates improper estimates that reflect sampling error around a proper structure, typically a negative error variance near zero in a small sample or for an item that nearly duplicates the factor, from those that reflect a misspecified or empirically underidentified model: the first kind needs no change of model, while the second calls for a different model rather than an estimate. One sample cannot always tell the two apart, so the function draws the line at what the coefficient can mean. When the error variances still sum to a nonnegative number, the model implies a nonnegative error variance for the composite and a model implied \(\omega\) between zero and one, so the coefficient is returned with a warning. When they sum to less than zero, the model implies a negative error variance for the composite and a model implied \(\omega\) above one, which no reliability coefficient can take; sampling error near a zero error variance does not produce this unless every item is nearly error free, and it is the signature of a solution that has run away, one error variance falling without bound as its loading grows. The function then stops with a message naming the item. So it does for three items whose correlations have a negative product: a single factor implies that the product of the three correlations equals the square of the product of the three loadings, so no real loadings reproduce them and the maximum likelihood estimate does not exist. Whatever the sum, a fit whose likelihood has no maximum, an error variance running off below zero while the likelihood is flat or still rising (checked by fitting the model again with the variance held further out, as fa_bifactor describes), stops the function with an error of class dmar_no_maximum that names the item and prints the lavaan code of the single-factor fit, where bounds = "pos.var" or a different model are the choices.

A bootstrap meets improper solutions more often than the sample does, since a resample can push an error variance that is near zero in the sample below it, which is a standardized loading past one (the fits are on the items' own metric, where a loading above one is routine). The argument improper governs the replications whose solution is improper but still yields a coefficient: "keep", the default, uses their estimates like any other, and "drop" sets them aside. Keeping is the default because setting them aside conditions the bootstrap distribution on admissibility and so trims its upper tail, the replications in which an error variance fell below zero; Yuan and Hayashi (2003) make the parallel argument for test statistics, counting a replication that fails because its resample lies far from the model rather than discarding it. A replication whose solution yields no coefficient is set aside under either setting. When its error variances sum below zero, the solution has run away and implies an \(\omega\) above one, beyond the top of the distribution like the improper replications kept. When three items have no single-factor solution, the side depends on the scale the resample is read on: on the estimator's own scale it continues the top of the distribution, since as a resample approaches that boundary one loading, and \(\omega\) with it, grows without bound, while its correlations, one of which is negative or zero, point to low reliability. The argument of Yuan and Hayashi does not settle it, since their extreme value belongs to a statistic that measures misfit and so has a direction, so such a replication is counted, on its own as well as among the improper ones, rather than placed on either side. A replication whose likelihood has no maximum is set aside as well, and counted among those that raised an error, under a message that names the item whose error variance ran off; the run goes on. Every such replication is counted in the bootstrap attribute and the printed line, and when the replications set aside and the improper ones kept together reach the tail area of the interval, \((1 - C)/2\) of B, a caution says that the limits depend on how they were treated. When some of them had no single-factor solution, the caution adds that the lower limit is likely too high: with three weakly related items the estimator itself runs high near that boundary, and the resamples beyond it are those whose correlations point to low reliability. When about half of the replications are improper, neither setting gives an interval worth reporting, and the counts are what the result can state.

Comparison with other packages. The psych package provides omega, which fits a Schmid-Leiman hierarchical factor model and reports several variants of \(\omega\) (\(\omega_t\), \(\omega_h\)) alongside extensive psychometric diagnostics. reliability_omega in DMAR differs in emphasis: it implements McDonald's \(\omega\) from a single-factor (congeneric) model and accompanies the point estimate with a confidence interval drawn from the methods compared in Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016). The same denominator distinction appears in semTools' compRelSEM() as its obs.var argument.

Examples

set.seed(113)
J <- 6
loadings <- seq(0.5, 0.8, length.out = J)
eta <- rnorm(200)
errors <- matrix(rnorm(200 * J), 200, J) %*% diag(sqrt(1 - loadings^2))
items <- sweep(matrix(rep(eta, J), 200, J), 2, loadings, `*`) + errors
colnames(items) <- paste0("y", seq_len(J))

# Default: robust omega, point estimate only (no bootstrap is run
# unless requested; a message names the call that produces the
# recommended interval).
reliability_omega(data = items)
#> Robust omega is reported without a confidence interval by default because its interval is bootstrap based. Request it with ci_method = "percentile" (or "bca"); B = 10000 replications is the default when you do.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.821
#>  se         <NA> 
#>  ci_lower   <NA> 
#>  ci_upper   <NA> 
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)

# The closed-form standard errors are derived under the model implied
# ratio, so with the observed denominator the interval comes from a
# bootstrap, which refits the single factor model once per
# replication. B = 10 keeps the example quick and is below the 400 a
# reported interval needs; the option lets it run and the warning says
# so. A reported interval deserves the default B = 10000, an accuracy
# choice rather than a formality (see Details). The percentile
# interval is what Kelley and Pornprasertmanit (2016) recommend for
# this coefficient, with ci_method = "bca" as the alternative, and
# seed makes the interval reproducible.
old <- options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE)
reliability_omega(data = items, ci_method = "percentile", B = 10,
                  seed = 113)
#> Warning: reliability_omega(): B = 10 is below the 400 replications a 95% interval is reported from (10 beyond each limit). The limits are shown because options(dmar.bootstrap_exploratory = TRUE) is set. With 10 replications each limit rests on about 0.3 of them and will move from seed to seed; use the result to explore or to demonstrate, and report an interval only from B of at least 400. B, B_used, and B_required are recorded in the result.
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.821
#>  se         0.016
#>  ci_lower   0.794
#>  ci_upper   0.840
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Denominator: observed composite variance (robust omega)
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)
#> 
#> Bootstrap: 10 replications attempted, 10 returned a value; at least 400 are required for a reported interval. Exploratory: below the number required for a reported interval
options(old)

# Model implied denominator with its closed-form robust ML interval,
# whose limits are formed on the logit scale; ci_method = "mlr" gives
# limits formed on the scale of omega.
reliability_omega(data = items, denominator = "model_implied")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.820
#>  se         0.019
#>  ci_lower   0.779
#>  ci_upper   0.854
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)

# Two further routes into the same coefficient. The first works from
# the summary statistics a paper reports, a covariance matrix and its
# sample size, with the maximum likelihood interval that summary
# input supports.
reliability_omega(S = cov(items), N = 200,
                  denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.820
#>  se         0.020
#>  ci_lower   0.781
#>  ci_upper   0.858
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)

# How much would a t reference lengthen that interval? On 30 degrees of
# freedom, an arbitrary small value chosen to show the effect, the
# limits move out a little; the line under the table says so.
reliability_omega(S = cov(items), N = 200,
                  denominator = "model_implied", ci_method = "ml",
                  wald_df = 30)
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.820
#>  se         0.020
#>  ci_lower   0.780
#>  ci_upper   0.860
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 200  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Wald interval: t reference on 30 degrees of freedom (wald_df), in place of the normal
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.043 (y2 with y5)

# The second is full information maximum likelihood with an auxiliary
# variable, where missingness on y2 depends on an auxiliary z (missing
# at random given z). Supplying aux implies missing = "fiml"; the
# N_complete row shows how many rows listwise deletion would have
# kept. With values missing, the interval can also refer to a t
# distribution on degrees of freedom taken from omega's own fraction of
# missing information, here in the fit that carries z (the calibration
# study behind the rule had no auxiliary variable, so this case rests
# on analogy; see Details); the line under the table gives N, the FMI,
# and the degrees of freedom that result. The rule is calibrated for
# limits on the scale of omega, so the interval here is the "mlr" one.
z <- eta + rnorm(200, sd = 0.5)
d <- data.frame(items, z = z)
d$y2[runif(200) < plogis(-1 + 1.5 * as.numeric(scale(z)))] <- NA
reliability_omega(data = d, aux = "z", denominator = "model_implied",
                  wald_df = "missing_information")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.819
#>  se         0.020
#>  ci_lower   0.780
#>  ci_upper   0.859
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 140  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Wald interval: t reference on 187.3 degrees of freedom, from von Hippel's (2016) max(3, N(1 - FMI) - 1) with N = 200 and FMI = 0.05845 (wald_df = "missing_information"), in place of the normal
#> 
#> The FMI degrees-of-freedom rule is approximate. Its calibration study admitted data sets that the affine-collapse screening sets aside, so coverage under that screening has not been established. See the method's help for its scope and conditional evidence.
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.075 (y2 with y5)

# Two-stage estimation instead: z enters only the first stage, where the
# means and covariances are estimated, and the interval uses the robust
# two-stage standard error, its limits again formed on the logit scale.
reliability_omega(data = d, aux = "z", missing = "two_stage",
                  denominator = "model_implied")
#>  term       value
#>  estimate   0.819
#>  se         0.020
#>  ci_lower   0.776
#>  ci_upper   0.855
#>  conf_level 0.950
#>  N          200  
#>  N_complete 140  
#>  n_items    6    
#> 
#> Denominator: composite variance implied by the fitted model
#> Largest residual correlation under the single-factor model: -0.070 (y2 with y5)
